works.title: Measuring stance dynamics in political debate using temporal graph neural networks
works.summary:
Zhou and Elejalde build TWLGCN, a temporal graph network that infers whether a Twitter user favours or opposes a referendum. It works on a user-hashtag graph rebuilt every 28 days, plus optional user-user edges. The model is trained on only 80 to 106 hashtags labelled by side, from Chile's 2020 and 2022 referendums (about 1.21M tweets; 12,237 and 4,934 users). Each period's embeddings carry into the next. This beats re-starting each period by 1.3% to 9.8% on the 2022 dataset. Mention, quote and reply edges add about 3% macro-F1; follower edges add little. Labels taken from hashtags agree with human coders (kappa 0.81 to 0.94, on 100 snapshots per dataset). The second half is descriptive: seven classes of movement per transition, with a "static" band of median + MAD; flip curves that mirror each other; and neighbours who tend to shift in the same direction (Fig. 6). There is no null baseline and no causal test.

This matters because `fec/stance/stance_dynamics.py` is an explicit port of this paper, without the GNN. It uses 91-day windows on the CU press corpus, carries a member's last stance through silent windows, uses the seven-dynamics taxonomy, tests whether neighbours move together, and proposes stances for silent members from their neighbours. Checked against the live output (`data/stance/stance_dynamics.json`), the port has three problems. The paper's static band assumes a continuous probability. On pooled stance signs it comes out at 0.708, so almost every move counts as static. The neighbour co-movement test is null (134 same / 122 opposite, 52%). The 77.5% sign agreement for imputation (n=1,087) has no party or majority-class baseline, while the paper scores with macro-F1 because its classes are imbalanced. The paper backs the design ideas. It does not validate carrying a label forward, the 91-day window, or the imputation. All of those remain UNVERIFIED.
works.question: Can a temporal graph neural network infer user-level stance (favor vs. against) toward a referendum from user-hashtag and user-user interaction graphs at each 28-day period, including users who never post about the target, and can the resulting trajectories characterize opinion shifts at population, individual and neighborhood levels? (Sec. 1.1, p.2-3.)
works.method: TWLGCN (Temporal Weighted LightGCN), an extension of WLGCN (Zhou & Elejalde, 2024). Each 28-day snapshot is a bipartite user-hashtag graph with count-weighted edges (Sec. 3.3). Four GCN propagation layers with symmetric degree normalization (Eq. 3), then multi-head attention over layer outputs (Eq. 4). User embeddings go to an MLP classifier with batch norm and dropout. Loss = focal loss (Eq. 5-6, class imbalance) + lambda1 * SSCL + lambda2 * ||H0||^2 (Eq. 11), with lambda1 = 1e-3 and lambda2 = 1e-6 (Sec. 4.1). SSCL, the Supervised Stance Contrastive Loss (Eq. 9-10), treats same-stance users and hashtags as positives and uses the adaptive reweighting alpha(x) = (rho + x)^(-lambda) from DynaDeno (Eq. 8). Noise-based augmentation of embeddings (Eq. 7). Sequential warm start: Xavier initialization at t=0; later periods inherit embeddings and MLP weights; hashtag initial embeddings from period-specific FastText (Sec. 3.3). User-user graphs: Pas (static follower/friend edges) and Act (per-period directed mention/quote/reply edges, Sec. 3.6, Eq. 12). Adam optimizer; max 1000 epochs; early stop after 50 epochs without validation macro-F1 gain. Stance probabilities from hashtag counts: p+ = |R+| / (|R+| + |R-|) (Eq. 1); ties are assigned by larger count, and ambiguous users are kept in training (p.6).

findings.finding: TWLGCN variants keep macro-F1 steady across periods, while the non-TWLGCN baselines (WLGCN, EvolveGCN, DynaDeno) fluctuate much more sharply.
findings.numbers: Steady 70%-90% macro-F1 over observed periods; exact baseline values are in Fig. 2 and Table S4 (supplement, not in text).

findings.finding: The abstract claims the model beats network-based baselines in macro-F1 by more than 5% at each period using only 0.2% labeled hashtags. The main text does not report the baseline gap numerically, so the claim cannot be checked from the text.
findings.numbers: Claimed >5%; labeled hashtags 80/171,615 (about 0.05%) in Entry_DS and 106/57,211 (about 0.19%) in Exit_DS (Table 1, p.5).

findings.finding: Carrying embeddings forward across snapshots matters: the full model beats the discrete variant that re-initializes embeddings each period.
findings.numbers: On Exit_DS, the full TWLGCN outperforms the discrete variant by 1.3% to 9.8%.

findings.finding: Adding active user-user relations (mentions, quotes, replies) gives the best overall performance. Passive follower/friend relations add little, and combining both does not help.
findings.numbers: Act improves the base model by about 3% on both datasets.

findings.finding: The supervised contrastive loss (SSCL) adds accuracy on top of focal loss. The authors attribute this to same-class contrastive signal.
findings.numbers: TWLGCN vs. TWLGCN w/o SSCL: about 2% gain in macro-F1.

findings.finding: Human annotators agree substantially with each other on the stance of user snapshots, and with hashtag-derived labels, which supports hashtags as a stance proxy.
findings.numbers: Human-human Cohen's kappa 0.836 (Entry_DS) and 0.842 (Exit_DS); human vs. hashtag-derived kappa 0.81 to 0.94; 100 user snapshots per dataset.
